accuracy.evidence: Checked every count against the multiples: 6 pairs of socks are 12, hops of 2 from 0 never land on an odd number like 7, 30p and 45p are 6 and 9 five-pence coins, and the tens on a 100 square all sit in the last column. The gap puzzles (6, 20, 40, 16) and all parameterised answers 2n, 5n and 10n match their stated working.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers report in Year 1 and 2 counting: dropping back into ones after a multiple (16 after 15, 11 after 10), giving the number of groups instead of the total (4 pairs means 4 shoes), skipping a step (25 after 15), and counting back in tens but slipping by one (39 or 29). Each of these has its own wrong option and message in the Challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagskip lab moves real groups: dragging sock pairs to a counted row that labels 2, 4, 6, a frog hopping on a 0 to 20 track with drawn arcs, 5p coins dropped into a purse to pay set amounts, colouring the tens on a 100 square, and filling gaps in rising and falling sequences. Highest shingle overlap with any other flag lab is 6.6 percent.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the jump size physical before naming it: the socks show that the number said is the total of objects, the frog track shows that 2s skip the odd numbers, the coin purse links counting in 5s to money, the 100 square shows the tens line up, and the gap puzzles include counting back in 2s so the pattern runs both ways.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before the matching task: whether the frog hopping in 2s will land on 7, what comes after 5, 10, 15 when paying with 5p coins, and whether the tens on the 100 square will make a straight line. The done message after each task checks the locked guess against what the child just saw.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge cycles six questions with the option order rotated, and every wrong choice gets its own explanation, for example 75 ends in 5 so it is in the 5s count but not the 10s, and 4 is how many pairs, each pair has 2 shoes so 8 shoes. Restart lets a child try the set again from the start.

readability.evidence: The kid text scores below grade 0 on Flesch-Kincaid with short sentences such as Say the last number of each jump, and every lab prompt is under twelve words. The adult notes score about grade 4.4 and use the curriculum terms multiples, count in steps and count forwards and backwards from the national curriculum wording.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph either gives a counting rule, an example with numbers, or a named slip to watch for. The adult notes name exact year groups and the specific errors (16 after 15, groups instead of total, 39 after 40) rather than general praise, and the pipeline filler check passed with no flagged phrases.

mobile.evidence: The lab uses the young layout with 56 pixel buttons, one action per step, and both tapping and dragging for socks and coins. The iPhone 13 and Android screenshots in light and dark show the frog track, coin purse and 100 square fitting inside the canvas with readable numbers and no clipped labels.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas has an aria-label naming the step, the answer row is a labelled group with a polite live status line, and every gesture task can be completed with the on-screen buttons alone. The browser gate ran axe in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13 and reported no violations.
